content.about:
About the Examination

The Bihar Public Service Commission (BPSC) Combined Competitive Examination (CCE) is the state-level examination for recruitment to various civil services and posts within the Government of Bihar. It is a comprehensive, multi-stage process designed to select the state's future administrative leaders. Regarded as one of the most prestigious state civil services exams in India, it serves as the gateway to a career in public service that directly impacts the governance and development of Bihar.

The Philosophy Behind the Examination

The BPSC CCE is engineered to assess more than just rote memorization. Its core philosophy is to identify individuals who possess a potent combination of intellectual depth, analytical acuity, ethical integrity, and a profound understanding of the state's socio-economic landscape. The examination seeks to evaluate a candidate's:

  • Critical Assimilation: The ability to understand complex information from diverse fields, filter out noise, and grasp the core issues relevant to the state and nation.
  • Balance of Judgment: The capacity to form reasoned opinions, consider multiple perspectives, and make sound, unbiased judgments.
  • Intellectual and Moral Integrity: A strong ethical compass and the courage to uphold constitutional and administrative values.
  • Leadership and Social Cohesion: The potential to lead and work collaboratively to solve pressing societal problems at the state level.
  • Awareness and Curiosity: A deep and abiding interest in local, state, national, and international affairs.

The Services at Stake

Successful candidates are allocated to various state-level services based on their rank and preferences. These services form the backbone of the state's administrative machinery.

Key Group 'A' & 'B' Services:

  • Bihar Administrative Service (BAS) - SDM/Dy. Collector
  • Bihar Police Service (BPS) - Dy. SP
  • State Tax Assistant Commissioner
  • Election Officer
  • Bihar Education Service
  • Registrar / Sub-Registrar
  • Labour Superintendent
  • District Audit Officer

And several others, including posts like Municipal Executive Officer, Revenue Officer, Block Panchayat Raj Officer, etc.

The Three-Tiered Selection Gauntlet

The CCE is a multi-layered process where each stage serves as a progressively finer filter to identify the most suitable candidates. The entire cycle, from notification to the final result, spans over a year.

  • Stage 1: Preliminary Examination (The Filter): This is an objective-type (Multiple Choice Questions) screening test. Its primary role is to eliminate non-serious candidates and select a manageable number for the Mains exam. It tests the breadth of a candidate's knowledge. Crucially, the marks from this stage are not counted for the final merit list. It is a pass/fail gateway to the next level.
  • Stage 2: Main Examination (The Crucible): Candidates who clear the Prelims undertake the Main Examination, a descriptive (written) exam that is the real test of intellectual depth and analytical skill. Spread over five papers (including qualifying ones), it evaluates a candidate's ability to articulate nuanced arguments and structure comprehensive answers. The marks from the Main Examination are the most significant component of the final score.
  • Stage 3: Personality Test (The Final Appraisal): The final stage is an interview conducted by a board of distinguished experts at the BPSC headquarters in Patna. The board, having access to the candidate's Detailed Application Form, assesses their personality, mental alertness, leadership qualities, and suitability for a high-stakes career in the state's public administration.

The Final Verdict: Merit and Allocation

The final merit list is prepared based on the total marks obtained in the Main Examination (900 marks) and the Personality Test (120 marks), for a grand total of 1020 marks. Based on their final rank, the preferences for services submitted by them, their category, and the vacancies available, candidates are allocated a service. This final allocation marks the successful culmination of one of the most demanding journeys in the Bihar state examination landscape.
content.timeline:
Typical Timeline (Indicative)

The BPSC CCE schedule can vary, but it generally follows a year-long cycle. Understanding this timeline is crucial for strategic planning and sustained preparation. The following is a typical, indicative schedule based on recent trends.

Disclaimer: These timelines are based on past trends. Always refer to the official BPSC calendar and notifications for the specific year for exact dates.

Phase 1: Notification & Application (June - August)

  • June / July: The official notification for the Combined Competitive Examination is released by BPSC on its website (bpsc.bih.nic.in). This document contains all essential details: vacancy numbers, eligibility, syllabus, and exam rules.
  • July - August: The online application window opens and typically remains active for about a month. This process involves a one-time registration (OTR) and filling out the application form. Aspirants must be careful while filling in details and uploading documents.

Phase 2: Preliminary Examination (September - October)

  • September: Approximately 2-3 weeks before the exam date, BPSC releases the e-Admit Card. Candidates must download and print it.
  • Late September / Early October: The Preliminary Exam is conducted on a single day. It consists of one paper of General Studies.

Phase 3: Prelims Result & Mains Application (November - December)

  • November: The results of the Preliminary Examination are typically declared within 4-6 weeks of the exam date. BPSC releases a list of the roll numbers of qualified candidates.
  • November - December: Shortly after the Prelims result, the qualified candidates are required to fill out the Detailed Application Form (DAF) for the Mains exam. This form collects detailed information and is also where candidates indicate their optional subject.

Phase 4: Main Examination (January - February)

  • December / January: Admit cards for the Main Examination are released for candidates who have successfully submitted their DAF.
  • January / February: The Main Examination is a descriptive (written) test conducted over 3-4 days.

Phase 5: Mains Result & Interview Schedule (May - June)

  • May / June: The results of the Main Examination are usually announced about 3 to 4 months after the exam. A list of candidates who have qualified for the Personality Test (Interview) is published.

Phase 6: Personality Tests (Interviews) (July - August)

  • The Personality Tests (Interviews) typically commence a few weeks after the Mains results are declared.
  • Candidates are summoned to the BPSC office in Patna in batches. The interview schedule is spread over several weeks.

Phase 7: Final Result Declaration (August - September)

  • This is the culmination of the entire process. The final merit list, based on the combined scores of the Main Examination and the Personality Test, is declared, usually within a few weeks of the conclusion of the last interview.
content.eligibility:
Eligibility Criteria

Before embarking on the rigorous journey of BPSC preparation, every aspirant must meticulously verify their eligibility. The criteria set by the Bihar Public Service Commission are strict and non-negotiable. Eligibility is primarily determined by four key parameters: Nationality, Age Limit, Educational Qualification, and Number of Attempts.

Note: The details provided here are based on prevailing rules. These are subject to change, and the official BPSC notification for the current examination year is the ultimate authority.

1. Nationality

A candidate must be a citizen of India to be eligible for the BPSC CCE.

2. Age Limit

The age of a candidate is calculated as of a specific cut-off date, which is typically the 1st of August of the examination year. The age limits vary depending on the post and category.

  • Minimum Age: 20, 21, or 22 years, depending on the service/post (e.g., 20 years for Dy. SP, 22 years for others like SDM).
  • Maximum Age: The upper age limit varies by category.

Age Relaxations (Upper Age Limit)

BPSC provides relaxations in the upper age limit for candidates from different categories:

Bihar Government Employees (continuous 3 years of service)5 Years relaxation

Note: Candidates must refer to the official notification for post-specific age requirements and detailed relaxation norms.

3. Educational Qualification

The minimum educational requirement is straightforward:

  • A candidate must hold a Bachelor's degree (Graduate) or an equivalent qualification from a recognized University.
  • Final-Year Students: Candidates who have appeared or intend to appear for their final degree examination and are awaiting results are also eligible to apply. However, they must have passed the exam by the time of filling the Mains application form.

4. Number of Attempts

The BPSC CCE is a meticulously designed three-stage process. Each stage has a distinct purpose and format. A thorough understanding of this pattern is the first step toward building a successful preparation strategy.

  • Merit Calculation: The cut-off for qualifying for the Main Examination is determined solely based on the marks scored in this paper.

Application Workflow

The application process for the BPSC CCE is conducted exclusively online through the official BPSC website (onlinebpsc.bihar.gov.in). It is a meticulous process that requires careful attention to detail. Any error can lead to the rejection of the application.

Stage 1: One-Time Registration (OTR)

Before filling out the application form, a candidate must complete the One-Time Registration. As the name suggests, this is a one-time activity.

  • Purpose: The OTR platform saves a candidate's basic personal information, which is used for all BPSC exam applications.
  • Information Required: You will need to provide your name, parents' names, date of birth, a valid mobile number, a valid email ID, Aadhaar number, and other basic details.
  • Verification: The mobile number and email ID are verified through OTPs. It is crucial to use an active and personal number and email.

Stage 2: Filling the Examination Application Form

Once your OTR is complete, you can log in and apply for the Combined Competitive (Preliminary) Examination.

1. Fee Payment:

  • Amount: Application fee is typically ₹600 for General category candidates.
  • Exemptions: The fee is reduced to ₹150 for SC/ST candidates of Bihar, permanent residents of Bihar (all categories of women), and persons with disabilities (40% or more).
  • Payment Modes: The fee can be paid online through Net Banking, or Credit/Debit cards.

2. Filling Details & Uploading Documents:

  • Personal & Educational Information: Fill in all required details carefully, ensuring they match your official documents.
  • Scanned Photograph & Signature: You need to upload a recent live webcam photo and scanned copies of your signature in Hindi and English. The documents must adhere to strict specifications mentioned in the notification.

Stage 3: Final Submission and Post-Submission Actions

  • Review and Submit: Before final submission, review the application preview carefully. Once submitted, changes are generally not possible outside the correction window.
  • Download Application PDF: After successful submission, download the system-generated PDF copy of your application form for your records.
  • Application Correction Window: BPSC may provide a brief window after the application period closes to allow candidates to make corrections.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Last-Minute Rush: Applying on the last day often leads to technical glitches and payment failures. Apply early.
  • Incorrect Photo/Signature: Uploading unclear images or documents not conforming to the specified format can lead to rejection.
  • Category Certificate Issues: Candidates claiming reservation must ensure their caste/residence/EWS/NCL certificates are issued by the competent authority of Bihar and are valid as per the notification.

After clearing the Prelims, candidates have to fill a separate Detailed Application Form (DAF) for the Mains exam, where they select their optional subject and provide service preferences.
content.syllabus:
Syllabus

The BPSC syllabus is the foundational document that dictates the scope of preparation. While it appears concise, each topic has a vast underlying scope.

The official notification from BPSC is the final authority on the syllabus. The following is a detailed breakdown as per the prevailing pattern.

Part A: Preliminary Examination Syllabus

General Studies (150 Marks)

This paper tests a candidate's general awareness and knowledge. Questions will be of a nature that a well-educated person can answer without specialized study.

  • General Science (General appreciation and understanding of science, including matters of everyday observation and experience).
  • Current events of national and international importance.
  • History of India and salient features of the History of Bihar.
  • General Geography and Geographical division of Bihar and its major river systems.
  • Indian Polity and Economy and major changes in the economy of Bihar in the post-independence period.
  • Indian National Movement and the part played by Bihar in it.
  • General Mental Ability.

Part B: Main Examination Syllabus

The Mains syllabus is extensive and requires in-depth, specialized study.

Paper 1: General Hindi (Qualifying)

The standard of this paper is of the level of Hindi taught in secondary schools of the Bihar School Examination Board. It is of a qualifying nature.

  • Essay (निबंध)
  • Grammar (व्याकरण)
  • Syntax (वाक्य विन्यास)
  • Summarization (संक्षेपण)

Paper 2: General Studies-I (300 Marks)

  • Modern History of India and Indian Culture: Covers the broad history of the country from the middle of the 19th century, with special focus on the history of Bihar, the introduction of Western education, the role of Bihar in the freedom struggle (including the Santhal Uprising, 1857 War of Independence, Champaran Satyagraha, Quit India Movement 1942), and features of Mauryan and Pal art and Patna Qalam painting.
  • Current Events of National and International Importance.
  • Statistical Analysis, Graphs and Diagrams: This section will include questions to test the candidate's ability to draw conclusions from statistical, graphical or diagrammatical information and to point out deficiencies, limitations or inconsistencies therein.

Paper 3: General Studies-II (300 Marks)

  • Indian Polity: Questions will be based on the political system in India, including Bihar.
  • Indian Economy and Geography of India: Questions will test knowledge on planning in India and the physical, economic, and social geography of India, with a focus on Bihar.
  • The Role and Impact of Science and Technology in the Development of India: Questions will test the candidate's awareness of the role and impact of science and technology in India and Bihar, with an emphasis on applied science.

Paper 4: Essay (300 Marks)

Candidates will be required to write an essay on one of several specified topics. The topics will often be related to philosophical themes, current affairs, and socio-economic issues, sometimes with a specific focus on Bihar (e.g., proverbs or 'LOKOKTI').

Paper 5: Optional Subject (100 Marks - Qualifying)

Candidates must choose one optional subject from a list provided by BPSC. This paper is MCQ-based and qualifying in nature. The syllabus for each optional subject is of the honours degree level. Aspirants must refer to the official BPSC notification for the detailed syllabus of their specific optional subject.
content.faqs:
Frequently Asked Questions

Here are answers to some of the most common questions about the BPSC Civil Services Examination.

Regarding Eligibility & Attempts

Can I apply for the exam while in the final year of my graduation?
Yes. You are eligible to appear for the Preliminary Exam. However, you must submit proof of passing your degree when you apply for the Main Examination.
What is the cut-off date for calculating the age limit?
The age limit is typically calculated as of the 1st of August of the notification year.
Do the marks from the Preliminary Exam count towards the final merit list?
No. The Preliminary Exam is purely a screening test. The final rank is based solely on the marks from the Main Examination (Written Merit Papers) and the Personality Test (Interview).
Is there negative marking in BPSC Prelims?
Yes. As per the new pattern, there is a negative marking of one-third (1/3rd) for every incorrect answer.

Regarding the Main Exam

What is the nature of the Optional Paper in Mains?
The Optional Paper in the BPSC Mains exam is now objective (MCQ-based) and qualifying in nature. Its marks are not added to the final merit list, but you must score the minimum qualifying marks to be eligible for final selection.
What is the weightage of the Essay paper?
The Essay paper holds significant weightage in the final merit list. It is for 300 marks, equal to the General Studies papers.

Regarding the Interview & Final Selection

What is the DAF (Detailed Application Form)?
The DAF is a comprehensive form filled by candidates who qualify for the Mains exam. It contains details about your academic, personal, and professional background. It is the primary source of information for the interview board.
How is the final rank determined?
The final rank is based on the grand total of marks obtained in the Main Examination (GS-I + GS-II + Essay = 900 marks) and the Personality Test (Interview - 120 marks), out of a total of 1020 marks.

content.about:
About the Examination

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) Civil Services Examination (CSE) is the unified national examination for recruitment to the premier civil services of India. It is not merely an academic test but a comprehensive, year-long process designed to select the nation's future administrative leaders. Regarded as one of the world's most challenging competitive exams, it serves as the gateway to a career in public service that directly impacts the governance, development, and international standing of the country.

The Philosophy Behind the Examination

The CSE is engineered to assess more than just rote memorization. Its core philosophy is to identify individuals who possess a potent combination of intellectual depth, analytical acuity, ethical integrity, and a profound sense of social commitment. The examination seeks to evaluate a candidate's:

  • Critical Assimilation: The ability to understand complex information from diverse fields, filter out noise, and grasp the core issues.
  • Balance of Judgment: The capacity to form reasoned opinions, consider multiple perspectives, and make sound, unbiased judgments under pressure.
  • Intellectual and Moral Integrity: A strong ethical compass, honesty, and the courage to uphold constitutional values.
  • Leadership and Social Cohesion: The potential to lead, inspire, and work collaboratively to solve pressing societal problems.
  • Awareness and Curiosity: A deep and abiding interest in the world around them, from local village issues to global geopolitical shifts.

The Services at Stake

Successful candidates are allocated to various services based on their rank and preferences. These services are broadly classified into two categories:

1. All India Services: These services are common to both the Union and State governments. Officers are recruited by the Centre but their services are placed under various State cadres, and they are liable to serve both the Centre and the States.

  • Indian Administrative Service (IAS)
  • Indian Police Service (IPS)

2. Central Civil Services (Group 'A' and 'B'): These services function directly under the Government of India and are involved in the administration of Union subjects.

Key Group 'A' Services:

  • Indian Foreign Service (IFS)
  • Indian Audit and Accounts Service (IA&AS)
  • Indian Revenue Service (IRS - Income Tax)
  • Indian Revenue Service (IRS - Customs & Indirect Taxes)
  • Indian Defence Accounts Service (IDAS)
  • Indian Postal Service (IPoS)

And several others.

The Three-Tiered Selection Gauntlet

The CSE is a multi-layered process where each stage serves as a progressively finer filter to identify the most suitable candidates. The entire cycle, from notification to the final result, spans over a year.

  • Stage 1: Preliminary Examination (The Great Filter): This is an objective-type (Multiple Choice Questions) screening test. With an application pool often exceeding a million candidates for roughly 10,000-15,000 Mains spots, its primary role is elimination. It tests the breadth of a candidate's knowledge and their aptitude for logical reasoning. Crucially, the marks from this stage are not counted for the final merit list. It is a pass/fail gateway to the next level.
  • Stage 2: Main Examination (The Crucible of Knowledge): Candidates who clear the Prelims undertake the Main Examination, a descriptive (written) exam that is the real test of intellectual depth and analytical skill. Spread over nine papers, it evaluates a candidate's ability to articulate nuanced arguments, structure comprehensive answers, and demonstrate mastery over their chosen optional subject. The marks from the Main Examination are the most significant component of the final score.
  • Stage 3: Personality Test (The Final Appraisal): The final stage is an interview conducted by a board of distinguished experts at the UPSC headquarters in New Delhi. It is explicitly described as a "purposive conversation" rather than a strict cross-examination. The board, having access to the candidate's Detailed Application Form (DAF), assesses their personality, mental alertness, leadership qualities, and suitability for a high-stakes career in public administration.

The Final Verdict: Merit and Allocation

The final merit list is prepared based on the total marks obtained in the Main Examination (1750 marks) and the Personality Test (275 marks), for a grand total of 2025 marks. Based on their final rank, the preferences for services submitted by them, their category, and the vacancies available, candidates are allocated a service and, for All India Services, a state cadre. This final allocation marks the successful culmination of one of the most demanding journeys in the Indian academic and professional landscape.
content.timeline:
Typical Timeline (Indicative)

The UPSC Civil Services Examination is a marathon that unfolds over a period of 14-15 months, from the date of notification to the start of the Foundation Course. Understanding this timeline is crucial for strategic planning, sustained preparation, and mental conditioning. The following is a typical, indicative schedule.

Disclaimer: These timelines are based on past trends. Always refer to the official UPSC calendar for the specific year for exact dates.

Phase 1: Notification & Application (February - March)

  • Early February: The official notification for the Civil Services Examination is released by UPSC on its website (upsc.gov.in). This document is the bible for aspirants, containing all essential details: vacancy numbers, eligibility criteria, syllabus, exam rules, and the list of examination centers.
  • February - March: The online application window opens on the day of the notification and typically remains active for about 20-25 days. This process involves a one-time registration (OTR) and filling out the application form in two parts. Aspirants must be extremely careful while filling in details, selecting centers (which are allotted on a first-apply-first-allot basis), and uploading documents.

Phase 2: Prelims Preparation & Admit Card (April - May)

  • April - May: This is a period of intense, focused preparation and revision for the Preliminary Examination.
  • Late April / Early May: Approximately 3-4 weeks before the exam date, UPSC releases the e-Admit Card for the Preliminary Examination. Candidates must download and print it. It is mandatory to carry the admit card along with a valid, original Photo ID to the examination hall.

Phase 3: Preliminary Examination (Late May / Early June)

  • The Preliminary Exam is conducted on a single day (usually a Sunday). It consists of two compulsory papers with a break in between.
    • Paper I: General Studies (9:30 AM to 11:30 AM)
    • Paper II: CSAT (2:30 PM to 4:30 PM)

Phase 4: Mains Qualification & DAF-I (July - August)

  • Mid to Late July: The results of the Preliminary Examination are typically declared within 30-40 days of the exam date. UPSC releases a list of the roll numbers of qualified candidates.
  • July - August: Shortly after the Prelims result, the qualified candidates are required to fill out the Detailed Application Form-I (DAF-I). This is an exhaustive form that collects detailed information about the candidate's personal background, educational qualifications, parental details, and employment history. It is also where candidates must indicate their optional subject for the Main Exam and provide preferences for services and cadres. This form is the basis for the interview later on.

Phase 5: Main Examination (September / October)

  • Late August / Early September: Admit cards for the Main Examination are released for candidates who have successfully submitted their DAF-I.
  • September / October: The Main Examination is a descriptive (written) test conducted over 5 days, usually spread across two weekends. It consists of 9 papers, testing the depth of a candidate's knowledge and analytical ability.

Phase 6: Personality Test Qualification & DAF-II (December - January)

  • December / Early January: The results of the Main Examination are usually announced about 2.5 to 3 months after the exam. A list of candidates who have qualified for the Personality Test (Interview) is published.
  • January: Qualified candidates are then required to fill the Detailed Application Form-II (DAF-II). This form often requires them to reconfirm their service preferences and provide additional details which might be used by the interview board.

Phase 7: Personality Tests (Interviews) (February - April)

  • The Personality Tests (Interviews) typically commence a few weeks after the Mains results are declared.
  • Candidates are summoned to the UPSC office (Dholpur House) in New Delhi in batches. The interview schedule is spread over several weeks, often concluding by mid or late Phase.

Phase 8: Final Result Declaration (Late April / May)

  • This is the culmination of the entire process. The final merit list, based on the combined scores of the Main Examination and the Personality Test, is declared. This usually happens within 5-10 days of the conclusion of the last interview.

Phase 9: Post-Result Formalities (June - August)

  • The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) undertakes the crucial task of service and cadre allocation based on ranks, preferences, category, and vacancies.
  • Late August / Early September: The Foundation Course for all newly recruited officers begins at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) in Mussoorie, officially starting their journey as civil servants.

Eligibility Criteria

Before embarking on the rigorous journey of UPSC preparation, every aspirant must meticulously verify their eligibility. The criteria set by the Union Public Service Commission are strict and non-negotiable. Eligibility is primarily determined by four key parameters: Nationality, Age Limit, Educational Qualification, and Number of Attempts.

Note: The details provided here are based on prevailing rules. These are subject to change, and the official UPSC notification for the current examination year is the ultimate authority.

1. Nationality

The nationality requirement varies depending on the service an individual aspires to join.

  • For Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), and Indian Foreign Service (IFS): The candidate must be a citizen of India. There are no exceptions for these premier services.
  • For all other services: The candidate must be one of the following:
    • A citizen of India, or
    • A subject of Nepal, or
    • A subject of Bhutan, or
    • A Tibetan refugee who came over to India before the 1st of January, 1962, with the intention of permanently settling in India, or
    • A person of Indian origin (PIO) who has migrated from Pakistan, Burma, Sri Lanka, East African countries of Kenya, Uganda, the United Republic of Tanzania, Zambia, Malawi, Zaire, Ethiopia and Vietnam with the intention of permanently settling in India.

Candidates belonging to the latter categories must possess a certificate of eligibility issued by the Government of India.

2. Age Limit

The age of a candidate is calculated as of a specific cut-off date, which is typically the 1st of August of the examination year. The general age limits are as follows:

  • Minimum Age: A candidate must have attained the age of 21 years.
  • Maximum Age: A candidate must not have attained the age of 32 years (for the General category).

This means a candidate from the General category must have been born not earlier than 2nd August, 1993 and not later than 1st August, 2004 (for the 2025 exam, as an example).

Age Relaxations (Upper Age Limit)

UPSC provides relaxations in the upper age limit for candidates belonging to reserved categories:

CategoryRelaxation in Upper Age LimitEffective Maximum Age
Scheduled Caste / Scheduled Tribe (SC/ST)5 Years37 Years
Other Backward Classes (OBC)3 Years35 Years
Defence Services Personnel (disabled in operations)3 Years35 Years
Ex-servicemen5 Years37 Years
Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD)10 Years42 Years

Note: Cumulative relaxations are generally not allowed. For instance, an OBC candidate with a benchmark disability can claim a relaxation of 10 years, not 10 + 3 years.

3. Educational Qualification

The minimum educational requirement is straightforward:

  • A candidate must hold a Bachelor's degree from any university incorporated by an Act of the Central or State Legislature in India or other educational institutions established by an Act of Parliament or declared to be deemed as a University under Section-3 of the UGC Act, 1956.
  • Alternatively, a candidate can possess an equivalent qualification.
  • Final-Year Students: Candidates who have appeared or intend to appear for their final degree examination and are awaiting results are also eligible to apply. However, they must produce proof of passing the said examination when they apply for the Main Examination.
  • Professional and technical qualifications recognized by the Government as equivalent to a professional and technical degree would also be sufficient.

4. Number of Attempts

The number of times a candidate can appear for the Preliminary Examination is limited. Appearing in even one paper of the Preliminary Exam is counted as an attempt.

CategoryNumber of Attempts
General / EWS6 Attempts
Other Backward Classes (OBC)9 Attempts
Scheduled Caste / Scheduled Tribe (SC/ST)Unlimited (subject to the age limit)
Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD)Unlimited for SC/ST, 9 for OBC, and 9 for General/EWS

An attempt is counted only if a candidate physically appears for at least one paper in the Preliminary Examination. Filling out the application form but not showing up for the exam does not count as an attempt.

Application Workflow

The application process for the UPSC CSE is conducted exclusively online through the official UPSC website. It is a meticulous process that requires careful attention to detail. Any error can lead to the rejection of the application. The process can be broken down into several key stages.

Stage 1: One-Time Registration (OTR)

Before filling out the application form for any UPSC examination, a candidate must complete the One-Time Registration. As the name suggests, this is a one-time activity.

  • Purpose: The OTR platform saves a candidate's basic personal information, which can then be automatically populated whenever they apply for a UPSC exam. This saves time and reduces the chance of errors in subsequent applications.
  • Information Required: You will need to provide your name, parents' names, date of birth, gender, minority status, a valid mobile number, a valid email ID, and details of your Class 10 board examination roll number.
  • Verification: The mobile number and email ID are verified through OTPs. It is crucial to use an active and personal mobile number and email, as all future communication from UPSC will be sent to them.
  • Permanence: The information submitted in the OTR profile is stored securely and can be updated, with some limitations, at any time.

Stage 2: Filling the Examination Application Form

Once your OTR is complete, you can log in and apply for the Civil Services (Preliminary) Examination. This is typically a two-part process.

Part-I Registration

This part involves filling in your essential details:

  • Personal Information: Most of this will be auto-filled from your OTR profile. You will need to confirm details and add information like your marital status and community (General, EWS, OBC, SC, ST).
  • Educational Qualification: You must provide details of your graduation degree.
  • Address and Contact Details: Confirmation of your mailing address.
  • Preference for Civil Services (Main) Examination: You will need to select your choice of optional subject and the language medium for the Mains examination at this stage.

Part-II Registration

  • Amount: A non-refundable application fee of ₹100 (Rupees One Hundred only).

  • Payment Modes: The fee can be paid through:
    • Online: Net Banking, UPI, or by using Visa/Mastercard/RuPay Credit/Debit cards.
    • Offline: "Pay-by-Cash" mode by generating a challan and depositing the cash at any branch of the State Bank of India (SBI).

2. Uploading of Photograph, Signature, and Photo ID Card:

This is a critical step where most errors occur. The documents must adhere to strict specifications.

  • Scanned Photograph: Must be a recent passport-style colour picture against a white or light-coloured background. The face should cover 3/4th of the photo's space. Format: JPG/JPEG. Size: 20 KB to 300 KB.
  • Scanned Signature: Must be signed with a black ink pen on white paper. Format: JPG/JPEG. Size: 20 KB to 300 KB.
  • Scanned Photo Identity Card: This must be the same ID you will bring to the exam hall (e.g., Aadhaar Card, Voter Card, PAN Card, Passport, Driving License). Format: PDF only. Size: 20 KB to 300 KB.

3. Examination Centre Selection:

  • UPSC allots examination centers on a "first-apply-first-allot" basis.
  • The capacity of popular centers fills up very quickly. It is highly advisable to complete your application as early as possible to secure your preferred city.

Stage 3: Final Submission and Post-Submission Actions

  • Review and Submit: Before final submission, the portal provides a complete preview of your application. Once submitted, changes are generally not possible outside the correction window.
  • Download Application PDF: After successful submission, download the system-generated PDF copy of your application form. It is essential to keep a soft and hard copy for your records.
  • Application Correction Window: UPSC usually provides a brief window (typically 7 days) after the application period closes to allow candidates to make corrections to their submitted forms. However, certain core fields might not be editable.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Last-Minute Rush: Applying on the last day often leads to technical glitches, payment failures, and mistakes. Apply early.
  • Incorrect Photo/Signature: Uploading selfies, blurred images, or documents not conforming to the specified size and format can lead to application rejection.
  • Spelling Mismatches: Ensure your name and parents' names match exactly with your Class 10 certificate.
  • OBC Certificate Issues: OBC candidates must ensure their Non-Creamy Layer (NCL) certificate is recent and valid for the specified financial year as per the notification.
  • Forgetting Final Submission: Completing Part-I but failing to complete Part-II (fee/uploads) means your application is incomplete and will be rejected.

After clearing the Prelims, candidates have to fill the Detailed Application Form (DAF-I), which is a much more exhaustive version of this application, forming the basis for the interview.

Syllabus

The UPSC syllabus is the foundational document that dictates the scope of preparation. While it appears concise, each topic has a vast underlying scope that requires sustained, multi-source study.

The official notification from UPSC is the final authority on the syllabus. The following is a summary breakdown as per the prevailing pattern.

Part A: Preliminary Examination Syllabus

Paper I: General Studies

  • Current events of national and international importance.
  • History of India and Indian National Movement.
  • Indian and World Geography - Physical, Social, Economic Geography of India and the World.
  • Indian Polity and Governance - Constitution, Political System, Panchayati Raj, Public Policy, Rights Issues, etc.
  • Economic and Social Development - Sustainable Development, Poverty, Inclusion, Demographics, Social Sector initiatives, etc.
  • General issues on Environmental Ecology, Bio-diversity and Climate Change.
  • General Science.

Paper II: Civil Services Aptitude Test (CSAT)

  • Comprehension.
  • Interpersonal skills including communication skills.
  • Logical reasoning and analytical ability.
  • Decision-making and problem-solving.
  • General mental ability.
  • Basic numeracy (numbers and their relations, orders of magnitude, etc.) and data interpretation (charts, graphs, tables, data sufficiency, etc. - Class X level).

Part B: Main Examination Syllabus

Paper I: Essay

Candidates are required to write essays on multiple topics, expected to keep closely to the subject and to arrange ideas in an orderly fashion.

Paper II: General Studies-I

Indian Heritage and Culture, History and Geography of the World and Society, including Indian art forms, modern Indian history from the 18th century, the freedom struggle, post-independence consolidation, world history, salient features of Indian society, and geography of the world.

Paper III: General Studies-II

Governance, Constitution, Polity, Social Justice and International Relations, including the Indian Constitution, functions and responsibilities of the Union and States, separation of powers, government policies, welfare schemes, and India's relations with its neighbours and the world.

Paper IV: General Studies-III

Technology, Economic Development, Bio-diversity, Environment, Security and Disaster Management, including Indian economy and planning, science and technology developments, environmental impact assessment, and internal security challenges.

Paper V: General Studies-IV

Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude, including the foundations of ethics in human actions, attitude, emotional intelligence, contributions of moral thinkers, ethics in public administration, and case studies on these topics.

Papers VI & VII: Optional Subject

Candidates choose one optional subject from a list of subjects provided by UPSC (e.g., Public Administration, Sociology, Geography, History, various Literatures, and technical subjects like Mathematics or Engineering disciplines). Each optional subject has two papers, and the syllabus is generally of the honours degree level. Aspirants must refer to the official UPSC notification for the detailed syllabus of their specific optional subject.
content.faqs:
Frequently Asked Questions

Here are answers to some of the most common questions and doubts that aspirants have about the UPSC Civil Services Examination.

Regarding Eligibility & Attempts

Can I apply for the exam while in the final year of my graduation?
Yes. You are eligible to appear for the Preliminary Exam if you are in your final year. However, you must submit proof of passing your degree when you apply for the Main Examination (i.e., by filling the DAF-I), failing which you will be disqualified.
What is the cut-off date for calculating the age limit?
The age limit is typically calculated as of the 1st of August of the examination year. For example, for CSE 2025, the cut-off date would be August 1, 2025.
What exactly counts as an "attempt"?
An attempt is counted if you physically appear for at least one paper (either GS Paper-I or CSAT) in the Preliminary Examination. Simply filling out the application form but not attending the exam does not count as an attempt. Disqualification or cancellation of candidature also counts as an attempt.
Is there a limit on attempts for OBC candidates who fall under the 'creamy layer'?
Yes. OBC candidates who belong to the 'creamy layer' are not entitled to reservation benefits, including age relaxation and extra attempts. They are treated as General category candidates and are thus limited to 6 attempts and an upper age limit of 32 years.

Regarding the Preliminary Exam

Is CSAT (Paper-II) compulsory?
Absolutely. You must appear for both papers of the Preliminary Exam. CSAT is qualifying in nature, meaning you must score a minimum of 33% (66/200 marks). If you do not clear the CSAT cut-off, your GS Paper-I will not be evaluated, and you will not qualify for the Mains.
Do the marks from the Preliminary Exam count towards the final merit list?
No. The Preliminary Exam is purely a screening test. Your score in Prelims is only used to determine if you qualify for the Main Examination. The final rank is based solely on the marks from the Main Examination (Written) and the Personality Test (Interview).
Is there negative marking in Prelims?
Yes. For every incorrect answer, one-third (1/3rd) of the marks assigned to that question are deducted. There is no penalty for unattempted questions.

Regarding the Main Exam

Can I write different papers of the Main Exam in different languages?
No. You must write all the merit papers (Essay, GS I-IV, and Optional Papers) in the single medium you have selected in your DAF-I. However, for the language papers (Paper A and Paper B), you must write them in the specified language (e.g., English for the English paper).
Are the qualifying language papers (Paper A & B) very difficult?
These papers are of Matriculation (Class X) standard and are designed to test basic language comprehension and expression. While they are qualifying, they should not be taken lightly. Failure to secure the minimum 25% marks in these papers will result in your other Mains papers not being evaluated.
How should I choose my optional subject?
Your choice of optional subject is a critical decision. Key factors to consider include: your interest and academic background in the subject, availability of study material and guidance, scoring trends in recent years, and the overlap of its syllabus with the General Studies papers.

Regarding the Interview & Final Selection

What is the DAF (Detailed Application Form)?
The DAF is a comprehensive form filled by candidates who qualify for the Mains and then the Interview. It contains details about your academic, personal, and professional background, including hobbies and service preferences. It is the primary source of information for the interview board and forms the basis for many of the questions asked.
Is the interview a test of knowledge?
Not primarily. The interview, or Personality Test, is designed to assess your personality, mental alertness, ethical standing, leadership qualities, and overall suitability for a career in the civil services. While awareness of current affairs is expected, the board is more interested in how you think than what you know.
How is the final rank determined?
The final rank is based on the grand total of marks obtained in the Main Examination (Written - 1750 marks) and the Personality Test (Interview - 275 marks), out of a total of 2025 marks.
Can I change my service or cadre preference after the final result?
No. The preferences for services and cadres submitted by you in the DAF are considered final. The allocation is done by the government (DoPT) based on your rank, preferences, category, and available vacancies. This allocation is final and cannot be changed.

content.about:
About the Examination

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) Engineering Services Examination (ESE) is the nationwide competitive examination for recruitment into the technical and managerial posts of the Government of India. It is a highly prestigious examination that selects graduate engineers for the nation's most vital technical services. Regarded as one of the toughest examinations in India for engineers, it serves as the gateway to a challenging and rewarding career, placing engineers at the forefront of national infrastructure development, technological advancement, and public utilities management.

The Philosophy Behind the Examination

The ESE is engineered to assess more than just theoretical knowledge. Its core philosophy is to identify individuals who possess a potent combination of deep technical expertise, robust analytical and problem-solving skills, and strong leadership potential. The examination seeks to evaluate a candidate's:

  • Technical Competence: A thorough and profound understanding of the fundamental principles of their engineering discipline.
  • Problem-Solving Ability: The capacity to apply engineering concepts to solve complex, real-world problems efficiently and innovatively.
  • Managerial Acumen: The potential to lead teams, manage large-scale projects, and make sound technical and administrative decisions under pressure.
  • Ethical Foundation: A strong sense of professional ethics, integrity, and a commitment to public service and national development.
  • Aptitude and General Awareness: A broad awareness of current affairs, general studies, and logical reasoning, which are essential for a well-rounded technocrat.

The Services and Disciplines

The ESE is conducted for recruitment into four main engineering disciplines. Successful candidates are allocated to various Group 'A' and Group 'B' services based on their rank, preferences, and the vacancies in their respective disciplines.

The four engineering disciplines are:

  • Category I: Civil Engineering
  • Category II: Mechanical Engineering
  • Category III: Electrical Engineering
  • Category IV: Electronics & Telecommunication Engineering

Some of the key services under these categories include:

  • Central Engineering Service
  • Indian Railway Service of Engineers (IRSE)
  • Indian Defence Service of Engineers
  • Central Power Engineering Service
  • Indian Skill Development Service
  • Indian Telecommunication Service

And many others across various ministries and departments.

The Three-Tiered Selection Gauntlet

The ESE is a multi-layered process where each stage is designed to filter candidates based on specific skills and knowledge. The entire cycle, from notification to the final result, spans over a year.

  • Stage 1: Preliminary Examination (The Technical Screen): This is an objective-type (Multiple Choice Questions) screening test comprising two papers. Paper-I tests General Studies and Engineering Aptitude, while Paper-II is discipline-specific. Its primary role is to select candidates with a solid foundation in both general and technical areas for the next stage. Crucially, the marks from this stage are not counted for the final merit list.
  • Stage 2: Main Examination (The Core Competency Test): Candidates who clear the Prelims undertake the Main Examination. This is a descriptive (written) exam consisting of two papers, both of which are entirely focused on the candidate's specific engineering discipline. It is the ultimate test of a candidate's in-depth technical knowledge, understanding of concepts, and ability to articulate complex engineering solutions. The marks from the Main Examination are the most significant component of the final score.
  • Stage 3: Personality Test (The Professional Appraisal): The final stage is an interview conducted by a board of experts at the UPSC headquarters in New Delhi. This interview assesses the candidate's suitability for a career in public service from a technical and managerial perspective. The board evaluates leadership qualities, initiative, intellectual curiosity, mental and physical energy, and other traits required for a successful career as an engineer in a government service.

The Final Verdict: Merit and Allocation

The final merit list is prepared based on the total marks obtained in the Main Examination (600 marks) and the Personality Test (200 marks), for a grand total of 800 marks. Based on their final rank in their specific engineering discipline, the preferences for services submitted by them, their category, and the vacancies available, candidates are recommended for appointment to various engineering services under the Government of India.
content.timeline:
Typical Timeline (Indicative)

The UPSC Engineering Services Examination is a marathon that unfolds over a period of 12-14 months, from the date of notification to the declaration of the final result. Understanding this timeline is crucial for strategic planning and sustained preparation. The following is a typical, indicative schedule based on past trends.

Disclaimer: These timelines are based on past trends. Always refer to the official UPSC calendar for the specific year for exact dates.

Phase 1: Notification & Application (September - October)

  • Mid to Late September: The official notification for the Engineering Services Examination is released by UPSC on its website (upsc.gov.in). This document contains all essential details: vacancy numbers, eligibility criteria, syllabus, exam rules, and the list of examination centers.
  • September - October: The online application window opens on the day of the notification and typically remains active for about 20-25 days. This process involves a one-time registration (OTR) and filling out the application form. Aspirants must be extremely careful while filling in their engineering discipline, selecting centers, and uploading documents.

Phase 2: Prelims Preparation & Admit Card (January - February)

  • November - January: This is a period of intense, focused preparation and revision for the Preliminary Examination.
  • Late January / Early February: Approximately 3 weeks before the exam date, UPSC releases the e-Admit Card for the Preliminary Examination. Candidates must download and print it.

Phase 3: Preliminary Examination (February)

  • The Preliminary Exam is conducted on a single day (usually a Sunday in February). It consists of two compulsory papers with a break in between.
    • Paper I: General Studies & Engineering Aptitude (10:00 AM to 12:00 PM)
    • Paper II: Engineering Discipline Specific (2:00 PM to 5:00 PM)

Phase 4: Mains Qualification & DAF-I (April - May)

  • Late March / Early April: The results of the Preliminary Examination are typically declared within 30-40 days of the exam date. UPSC releases a list of the roll numbers of qualified candidates.
  • April - May: Shortly after the Prelims result, the qualified candidates are required to fill out the Detailed Application Form-I (DAF-I). This is an exhaustive form that collects detailed information about the candidate's personal background, educational qualifications, and service preferences. This form is the basis for the interview later on.

Phase 5: Main Examination (June / July)

  • May / June: Admit cards for the Main Examination are released for candidates who have successfully submitted their DAF-I.
  • June / July: The Main Examination is a descriptive (written) test conducted on a single day, with two sessions for the two discipline-specific papers. It tests the depth of a candidate's technical knowledge and problem-solving ability.

Phase 6: Personality Test Qualification (September / October)

  • September / October: The results of the Main Examination are usually announced about 2 to 3 months after the exam. A list of candidates who have qualified for the Personality Test (Interview) is published.

Phase 7: Personality Tests (Interviews) (October - December)

  • The Personality Tests (Interviews) typically commence a few weeks after the Mains results are declared.
  • Candidates are summoned to the UPSC office (Dholpur House) in New Delhi in batches. The interview schedule is spread over several weeks.

Phase 8: Final Result Declaration (December / January)

  • This is the culmination of the entire process. The final merit list, based on the combined scores of the Main Examination and the Personality Test, is declared. This usually happens within 10-15 days of the conclusion of the last interview.
content.eligibility:
Eligibility Criteria

Before embarking on the rigorous journey of UPSC ESE preparation, every aspirant must meticulously verify their eligibility. The criteria set by the Union Public Service Commission are strict and non-negotiable. Eligibility is primarily determined by three key parameters: Nationality, Age Limit, and Educational Qualification.

Note: The details provided here are based on prevailing rules. These are subject to change, and the official UPSC notification for the current examination year is the ultimate authority.

1. Nationality

A candidate for the Engineering Services Examination must be one of the following:

  • A citizen of India, or
  • A subject of Nepal, or
  • A subject of Bhutan, or
  • A Tibetan refugee who came over to India before the 1st of January, 1962, with the intention of permanently settling in India, or
  • A person of Indian origin (PIO) who has migrated from Pakistan, Burma, Sri Lanka, East African countries of Kenya, Uganda, the United Republic of Tanzania, Zambia, Malawi, Zaire, Ethiopia and Vietnam with the intention of permanently settling in India.

Candidates belonging to the latter categories must possess a certificate of eligibility issued by the Government of India.

2. Age Limit

The age of a candidate is calculated as of a specific cut-off date, which is typically the 1st of January of the examination year. The general age limits are as follows:

  • Minimum Age: A candidate must have attained the age of 21 years.
  • Maximum Age: A candidate must not have attained the age of 30 years (for the General category).

This means a candidate from the General category must have been born not earlier than 2nd January, 1996 and not later than 1st January, 2005 (for the 2026 exam, as an example).

Age Relaxations (Upper Age Limit)

UPSC provides relaxations in the upper age limit for candidates belonging to reserved categories:

CategoryRelaxation in Upper Age LimitEffective Maximum Age
Scheduled Caste / Scheduled Tribe (SC/ST)5 Years35 Years
Other Backward Classes (OBC)3 Years33 Years
Defence Services Personnel (disabled in operations)3 Years33 Years
Ex-servicemen5 Years35 Years
Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD)10 Years40 Years

3. Educational Qualification

This is the most critical eligibility criterion for ESE. The minimum educational requirement is:

  • A candidate must have obtained an Engineering Degree from a University incorporated by an Act of the Central or State Legislature in India or other Educational Institutions established by an Act of Parliament or declared to be deemed as Universities under Section 3 of the University Grants Commission Act, 1956.
  • Alternatively, a candidate must have passed Sections A and B of the Institution Examinations of the Institution of Engineers (India).
  • Obtained a degree/diploma in Engineering from such foreign University/College/Institution and under such conditions as may be recognised by the Government for the purpose from time to time.
  • Passed Graduate Membership Examination of the Institution of Electronics and Telecommunication Engineers (India).
  • Passed Associate Membership Examination Parts II and III/Sections A and B of the Aeronautical Society of India.
  • Final-Year Students: Candidates who have appeared or intend to appear for their final degree examination and are awaiting results are also eligible to apply. However, they must produce proof of passing the said examination along with the Detailed Application Form (DAF-I) for the Main Examination.

The degree must be in one of the four eligible disciplines: Civil, Mechanical, Electrical, or Electronics & Telecommunication Engineering.

4. Number of Attempts

There is no restriction on the number of times a candidate can appear for the ESE. Candidates can attempt the examination as many times as they wish, provided they fulfill the age limit and other eligibility criteria specified in the examination notification.

content.syllabus:
Syllabus

The syllabus for the ESE is discipline-specific, but Paper I of the Preliminary Examination is common to all candidates. The standard of Paper I is such as may be expected of an Engineering or Science Graduate, while the standard of the discipline-specific papers is approximately that of an Engineering Degree Examination of an Indian University.

Preliminary Examination: Paper I - General Studies and Engineering Aptitude (200 Marks, Common to All)

This objective-type paper is common to candidates of all four engineering disciplines and covers the following ten topics:

  • Current issues of national and international importance relating to social, economic and industrial development.
  • Engineering Aptitude covering Logical reasoning and Analytical ability.
  • Engineering Mathematics and Numerical Analysis.
  • General Principles of Design, Drawing, Importance of Safety.
  • Standards and Quality practices in production, construction, maintenance and services.
  • Basics of Energy and Environment: Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, Climate Change, Environmental impact assessment.
  • Basics of Project Management.
  • Basics of Material Science and Engineering.
  • Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) based tools and their applications in Engineering such as networking, e-governance and technology based education.
  • Ethics and values in the Engineering profession.

Note: Questions from all 10 topics are set, with marks for each topic ranging from 5% to 15% of the total marks in the paper. No special study is expected beyond the knowledge of an engineering graduate.

Preliminary Examination: Paper II & Main Examination (Discipline-Specific)

Paper II of the Preliminary Exam and both papers of the Main Examination are entirely focused on the candidate's chosen engineering discipline, covering the core subjects of that stream in depth. A broad outline of the technical areas covered for each discipline is given below.

  • Civil Engineering: Building Materials, Structural Engineering, Soil Mechanics and Foundation Engineering, Fluid Mechanics, Hydraulics, Surveying, Environmental Engineering, Highway and Railway Engineering, and Construction Management.
  • Mechanical Engineering: Thermodynamics, Fluid Mechanics, Strength of Materials, Theory of Machines, Machine Design, Engineering Materials, Manufacturing Science, Industrial Engineering, and Power Plant Engineering.
  • Electrical Engineering: Circuit Theory, Electrical Machines, Power Systems, Control Systems, Electrical and Electronic Measurements, Analog and Digital Electronics, and Power Electronics.
  • Electronics & Telecommunication Engineering: Basic Electronics Engineering, Signals and Systems, Networks, Analog and Digital Electronics, Control Systems, Communication Systems, Microwave Engineering, and Computer Networks.

For the exact, topic-wise breakdown of the discipline-specific syllabus, candidates should refer to the detailed syllabus published in the official UPSC ESE notification for their engineering stream.

Frequently Asked Questions

Regarding Eligibility & Attempts

Can I apply for the ESE in the final year of my engineering degree?

Is there a limit on the number of attempts for the ESE?
No. There is no restriction on the number of attempts. Candidates can attempt the examination as many times as they wish, provided they fulfill the age limit and other eligibility criteria specified in the examination notification.

Yes. For each wrong answer marked by a candidate in the objective-type papers, one-third (1/3rd) of the marks assigned to that question are deducted. There is no penalty for unattempted questions.

Regarding the Main Exam & Interview

Are scientific calculators allowed in the Main Examination?
Yes. Candidates are permitted to use non-programmable scientific calculators for the Main Examination. This is a crucial tool for solving the complex numerical problems that are a major part of the descriptive papers.
Are there any language or essay papers in ESE Mains?
No. The ESE Main Examination is purely technical. It consists of only two descriptive papers from your specific engineering discipline. There are no qualifying language papers or general essay papers.
What is the DAF (Detailed Application Form)?
The DAF is a comprehensive form filled by candidates who qualify for the Mains. It contains details about your academic, personal, and professional background, including projects, hobbies, and service preferences. It is the primary source of information for the interview board.
How is the final rank determined?
The final rank is based on the grand total of marks obtained in the Main Examination (Written - 600 marks) and the Personality Test (Interview - 200 marks), out of a total of 800 marks. The merit list is prepared separately for each of the four engineering disciplines.

content.about:
About the Examination

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) Examination is a national-level competitive exam for the recruitment of Assistant Commandants (AC), who are Group 'A' officers. This examination serves as the unified gateway for aspiring candidates to join the officer cadre of India's premier internal security forces. It is a highly respected career path that offers a unique blend of adventure, responsibility, and service to the nation.

The Philosophy Behind the Examination

The CAPF (AC) examination is designed to select disciplined, dynamic, and resilient leaders. Beyond academic knowledge, the selection process rigorously assesses a candidate's physical and mental fortitude, integrity, and suitability for command roles in challenging operational environments. The exam seeks individuals who possess:

  • Physical and Mental Robustness: The ability to endure tough physical conditions and maintain composure under extreme pressure.
  • Leadership and Command Quality: The potential to lead a company of armed personnel, make critical decisions, and inspire confidence.
  • Intellectual Acuity: A strong grasp of general awareness, analytical reasoning, and security-related issues.
  • Unwavering Integrity: A strong moral compass and a deep sense of patriotism and duty.

The Forces at Stake

Successful candidates are appointed as Assistant Commandants in one of the five Central Armed Police Forces under the Ministry of Home Affairs. These forces are the pillars of India's internal security architecture:

  • Border Security Force (BSF)
  • Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF)
  • Central Industrial Security Force (CISF)
  • Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP)
  • Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB)

The Three-Stage Selection Process

The CAPF (AC) selection is a multi-stage process designed to comprehensively evaluate a candidate's fitness for the role. The entire cycle spans over a year.

  • Stage 1: Written Examination: This is the first filter and consists of two papers conducted on the same day. Paper I is an objective test of General Ability and Intelligence, while Paper II is a descriptive test of General Studies, Essay, and Comprehension. This stage assesses the academic and analytical capabilities of the candidates.
  • Stage 2: Physical Standards Test (PST) / Physical Efficiency Test (PET) & Medical Standards Test: Candidates who qualify the written exam are called for this stage. The PST involves checking physical parameters like height and chest. The PET includes a series of athletic events to test physical endurance and agility. This is followed by a detailed medical examination to ensure candidates meet the stringent health requirements. This stage is qualifying in nature.
  • Stage 3: Interview / Personality Test: The final stage is an interview conducted by a board of senior officers and experts at the UPSC. This test assesses the candidate's personality, leadership potential, communication skills, and overall suitability for a command position in the armed police forces.

The Final Verdict: Merit and Allocation

The final merit list is prepared based on the total marks obtained in the Written Examination (450 marks) and the Interview/Personality Test (150 marks), for a grand total of 600 marks. Based on their final rank and the preferences submitted by them, candidates are allocated to one of the five CAPFs.

content.syllabus:

The syllabus for the CAPF (AC) exam is designed to test a candidate's broad-based knowledge and analytical skills.

Paper I: General Ability and Intelligence (250 Marks)

  • General Mental Ability: Logical Reasoning, Quantitative Aptitude (including Numerical Ability and Data Interpretation).
  • General Science: General awareness, scientific temper, comprehension and appreciation of scientific phenomena of everyday observation including new areas of importance like Information Technology, Biotechnology, Environmental Science.
  • Current Events of National and International Importance: Knowledge of current events of national and international importance in the spheres of culture, music, arts, literature, sports, governance, societal and developmental issues, industry, business, globalisation, and interplay among nations.
  • Indian Polity and Economy: India's political system and the Constitution of India, social systems and public administration, economic development in India, regional and international security issues and human rights including its indicators.
  • History of India: Social, economic and political aspects of the History of India. Also includes the areas of growth of nationalism and freedom movement.
  • Indian and World Geography: Physical, social and economic aspects of geography pertaining to India and the World.

Paper II: General Studies, Essay and Comprehension (200 Marks)

Part-A: Essay (80 Marks)

Candidates have to write descriptive essays on given topics. The topics are related to modern Indian history especially of the freedom struggle, geography, polity and economy, knowledge of security and human rights issues, and analytical ability. The essays can be written in either English or Hindi.

Part-B: Comprehension, Précis Writing, etc. (120 Marks)

This part consists of Comprehension passages, précis writing, developing counter arguments, report writing, and language/grammar based questions. This part must be attempted in English only.

Frequently Asked Questions

Here are answers to some common questions about the UPSC CAPF (AC) Examination.

Regarding Eligibility & Application

Can I apply for the CAPF exam in the final year of my graduation?
Yes. You are eligible to apply, but you must produce proof of passing your degree at the time of submitting the Detailed Application Form (DAF), which is after the written exam result.
Is there a limit on the number of attempts?
No. There is no limit on the number of attempts, provided you fulfill the age criteria. You can appear for the exam as many times as you want between the ages of 20 and 25 (with relaxations for reserved categories).
Are there any relaxations in height for candidates from hilly regions?
Yes. Relaxations in physical standards, including height, are available for candidates belonging to specified categories like Garhwalis, Kumaonis, Gorkhas, and those from certain North-Eastern states, as detailed in the official notification.

Regarding the Examination

Is there negative marking in both papers?
No. Negative marking of 1/3rd of the marks is applicable for incorrect answers in Paper I only. There is no negative marking in the descriptive Paper II.
Can I write the entire Paper II in Hindi?
No. Only Part-A (Essay) of Paper II can be written in either English or Hindi. Part-B (Comprehension, Précis Writing, etc.) must be attempted in English only.
What happens if I fail the Physical Efficiency Test (PET)?
Failure to qualify in any of the PET events will lead to immediate disqualification. Your candidature for that year's examination will be cancelled, and you will not proceed to the medical examination or interview stage.

About the Examination

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) Combined Defence Services (CDS) Examination is a prestigious national-level exam conducted twice a year to recruit Commissioned Officers into the Indian Armed Forces. Unlike civilian services, the CDS exam is the primary gateway for university graduates to embark on a challenging and honourable career leading the men and women of the Indian Army, Navy, and Air Force.

The Philosophy Behind the Examination

The CDS selection process is designed to identify candidates who possess the unique blend of attributes required for military leadership, often summarized as "Officer Like Qualities" (OLQs). The exam assesses more than academic knowledge; it seeks individuals with:

  • Mental Robustness & Aptitude: The ability to think clearly, solve problems logically, and perform under pressure.
  • Physical Fitness & Courage: A high standard of physical and mental endurance to meet the demanding nature of military life.
  • Leadership & Integrity: The potential to lead, inspire confidence, and uphold the highest standards of honour and integrity.
  • Patriotism & Sense of Duty: A deep-seated commitment to the nation and an unwavering sense of duty and responsibility.

The Academies at Stake

Successful candidates are admitted to different defence academies based on their preference and merit. The CDS exam serves as the entry point for the following prestigious institutions:

  • Indian Military Academy (IMA), Dehradun
  • Indian Naval Academy (INA), Ezhimala
  • Air Force Academy (AFA), Hyderabad
  • Officers Training Academy (OTA), Chennai (Men & Women)

The Two-Stage Selection Process

The CDS selection is a comprehensive two-stage process designed to thoroughly evaluate a candidate's suitability for a commission in the Armed Forces.

  • Stage 1: Written Examination: This is an objective-type (MCQ) examination designed to test the candidate's knowledge of English, General Knowledge, and Elementary Mathematics. It serves as a screening test to select candidates for the next stage. Candidates applying only for the Officers' Training Academy (OTA) are exempted from the Mathematics paper.
  • Stage 2: Services Selection Board (SSB) Interview: Candidates who qualify in the written exam are called for the SSB Interview. This is an intensive 5-day personality and intelligence assessment. It includes a battery of psychological tests, group tasks, and a personal interview to evaluate a candidate's "Officer Like Qualities" (OLQs). This stage is the ultimate test of one's character, leadership potential, and mental fortitude.

The Final Verdict: Merit and Joining Instructions

A final merit list is prepared based on the total marks obtained in the Written Examination and the SSB Interview. Candidates who clear the medical examination are issued joining instructions for their respective academies based on their rank, preferences, and the number of vacancies available.
content.timeline:
Typical Timeline (Indicative)

The CDS Examination is conducted biannually, providing two opportunities each year for aspiring candidates. The two cycles are referred to as CDS (I) and CDS (II). The timeline for each cycle spans approximately 9-10 months from notification to the commencement of the course.

Disclaimer: These timelines are illustrative. Always refer to the official UPSC calendar for exact dates.

Typical Timeline for a Single CDS Cycle

  • Phase 1: Notification & Application (e.g., Oct-Nov for CDS I / May-Jun for CDS II): The official notification is released by UPSC, and the online application window opens for about 20-25 days.
  • Phase 2: Admit Card Release (e.g., Jan-Feb for CDS I / Aug for CDS II): E-Admit cards are made available for download from the UPSC website around 3 weeks before the exam date.
  • Phase 3: Written Examination (e.g., Feb or Apr for CDS I / Sep for CDS II): The objective-type written exam is conducted on a single day across various centers in India.
  • Phase 4: Written Examination Result (e.g., Mar-May for CDS I / Oct-Nov for CDS II): UPSC declares the results of the written exam, publishing a list of qualified candidates' roll numbers.
  • Phase 5: SSB Interview Process (Spans Several Months): Qualified candidates are allotted dates for their 5-day SSB interviews. This phase is conducted by the respective services (Army, Navy, Air Force) and can take place over several months following the written result.
  • Phase 6: Final Result Declaration (e.g., Jul-Aug for CDS I / Feb-Mar for CDS II): A final merit list is published, containing the names of candidates recommended after the SSB interviews.
  • Phase 7: Course Commencement (e.g., Jan for CDS I / Jul for CDS II): Following medical examinations and other formalities, the course commences at the respective training academies.

The CDS selection process is a two-stage affair: a written exam followed by an SSB interview for qualified candidates.

Key Features of the Written Stage

  • Negative Marking: There is a penalty for wrong answers. One-third (0.33) of the marks assigned to a question will be deducted for each incorrect answer.
  • Language of Paper: The question papers for General Knowledge and Elementary Mathematics will be set bilingually in Hindi as well as English.

Stage 2: Services Selection Board (SSB) Interview

This is a comprehensive personality and intelligence test conducted over 5 days. It is not an academic knowledge test but an evaluation of "Officer Like Qualities" (OLQs). The SSB process is divided into two stages.

  • Stage I (Screening): This is a one-day screening process involving an Officer Intelligence Rating (OIR) test and a Picture Perception & Description Test (PPDT). Candidates who clear Stage I proceed to Stage II.
  • Stage II (Main Tests): This stage lasts for the remaining four days and includes:
    • Psychological Tests: Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), Word Association Test (WAT), Situation Reaction Test (SRT), and Self Description Test (SD).
    • Group Testing Officer (GTO) Tasks: A series of indoor and outdoor group exercises, including group discussions, group planning exercises, and command tasks.
    • Personal Interview: A one-on-one conversation with a senior officer (the Interviewing Officer).
    • Conference: On the final day, all assessors jointly discuss each candidate's performance before finalizing their recommendation.

Final Merit Calculation

The final merit list is prepared based on the combined marks of the Written Exam and the SSB Interview.

For IMA, INA, AFA: Written Exam (300) + SSB Interview (300) = Total 600 Marks

For OTA: Written Exam (200) + SSB Interview (200) = Total 400 Marks
